ns_lorraine_head.blurb: A seaside cliff on Cape Breton Island, in the Sydney district, with fourteen routes on volcanic tuff. Trad lines outnumber bolted ones roughly two to one, and the grades start around 5.6, bunch up between 5.8 and 5.11, and top out at 5.12. The stone is smooth and solid, with crisp edges and cracks, though how it feels shifts from one section to the next. Best for climbers who already lead comfortably at 5.8 to 5.10 and want a quiet spot on the Atlantic shore.

ns_2a_lunchbucket_ledge.blurb: A set of stacked ledges on the Mainface cliff, sitting above the Mr. Puff section, with thirteen routes. Ten are trad and three are sport, and the grades run from the 5.7 range up to a single 5.12, with most lines between 5.8 and 5.10. Moving between the tiers takes some scrambling, and loose rock is reported on one of the scrambles, so it suits climbers who are relaxed on easy ground. The cliff as a whole is the largest on the mainland and carries the only multi-pitch climbing near Halifax.

ns_4_arch_wall.blurb: One of six walls at Columbus Wall, a group of cliffs tucked into forest near Musquodoboit. The Arch Wall holds thirteen routes, every one of them trad, from about 5.6 through the 5.11 range, with 5.10 the most common grade. The surrounding trees keep the wind off, so it feels sheltered, but bugs and warmer temperatures come with that. Anchors are mostly fixed rings, though a tree sling is sometimes needed. A good pick for climbers working on their gear skills at 5.9 and 5.10 on a forested crag.

ns_upper_pools_east_bank.blurb: A winter ice section on the Folly River in Nova Scotia, one of three areas that make up the Folly River crag. It has twelve water-ice routes, ten at WI3 and two at WI4, and a few are set up as top-ropes. That makes it a good fit for climbers stepping into moderate ice. The crag as a whole is known for a dense cluster of easy and moderate lines, mostly about fifteen metres tall, and it sits close to the highway, so a day trip is simple. It can draw crowds on busy weekends.

ns_the_back_slabs.blurb: A gently angled, polished slab marked by faint grooves and small steps, with a single blocky overhang, tucked behind the main cliff at Eagle's Nest, the urban crag by Bedford, close to Halifax. Twelve routes mix trad, bolted sport lines and top-rope options. Grades run from 5.5 to 5.10, and most lines sit between 5.5 and 5.8, making it a friendly place for newer leaders and anyone building up slab technique. A few harder ones around 5.10 give stronger climbers something to try.
ns_the_back_slabs.parking_note: Leave the car in the dead-end lane just right of Snowy Owl Drive, reached from Highway 7 via Golf Links Road, Eaglewood Drive and Condor Road.

ns_crow_s_nest.blurb: A hard trad cliff on Nova Scotia's Atlantic coast near Terrance Bay, lightly visited because getting there is a trek. All twelve routes are trad: one around 5.8, one around 5.9, a handful at 5.10 and a clear majority at 5.11. The rock is sharp and cracked, and the wall leans out slightly, so lines feel steeper and pumpier than the number suggests. Gear is usually plentiful, and sea air keeps it cool. This is a destination for strong crack climbers rather than beginners.

ns_railway_crag.blurb: A small crag in the Musquodoboit area of Nova Scotia, beneath a landmark known locally as Skull Rock. It has twelve routes, eight trad and four sport, with grades from 5.6 up to 5.12. Most of the lower grades are trad, and the harder climbs are bolted. Boulders sit at the base, and young birch and maple provide summer shade until the routes rise above the trees partway up. The rock stays mostly dry and the crag is rarely crowded. Bring bug spray in summer.

ns_5a_high_ledge.blurb: A ledge high on the North Buttress of the Mainface cliff, with eleven trad routes. Many are upper pitches of older full-length climbs, and some newer pitches start from the ledge itself. The grades run from one very easy line up to about 5.10, with most between 5.8 and 5.10. Getting onto the ledge involves reaching the rappel station and then scrambling down a small ledge, so it suits climbers comfortable with exposure. It sits on the largest cliff on the mainland, which also offers the only multi-pitch climbing near Halifax.
